CausalChain: Hepatic PPARβ/δ activation -> Increased lipogenic enzyme expression (e.g., ACC1) -> Elevated de novo synthesis of PC(18:0/18:1) -> Secretion of PC(18:0/18:1) into circulation -> Uptake by skeletal muscle -> Activation of muscle PPARα -> Enhanced muscle fatty acid oxidation -> Reduced circulating TAG and improved metabolic profile; Additionally, hepatic PPARα activation -> Upregulation of FGF21 -> Systemic enhancement of insulin sensitivity. Moderated hepatic PPARγ activity prevents excessive lipid storage in hepatocytes, completing the balanced network.
Hypothesis: Balanced modulation of hepatic PPAR isoforms—specifically co-activation of PPARβ/δ and PPARα together with moderated PPARγ activity—produces a coordinated increase in lipid mediators (PC(18:0/18:1)) and hepatokines (FGF21) that enhance skeletal muscle fatty acid oxidation via PPARα, thereby ameliorating dyslipidemia and insulin resistance in metabolic syndrome and NAFLD.
Abstract: This study proposes a novel mechanism by which fine‐tuning hepatic PPAR isoform activities can coordinate inter‐organ communication to improve systemic metabolic homeostasis. We hypothesize that a balanced activation of hepatic PPARβ/δ and PPARα—while concurrently tempering PPARγ activity—modulates the synthesis and secretion of key lipid mediators, in particular phosphatidylcholine (18:0/18:1) and the hepatokine FGF21. These signaling molecules may in turn stimulate PPARα activity in skeletal muscle, enhancing fatty acid uptake and β-oxidation, thereby reducing circulating triglycerides and improving insulin sensitivity. This multi‐faceted regulatory network may serve as a promising therapeutic target for metabolic syndrome and NAFLD.
